title: Build a brand voice checker for everything you ship
description: A system that scores any draft against your brand voice guide and flags the exact lines that read generic or off-tone before it ships.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

triage.title: Triage
triage.content: Sorting items by urgency or importance to decide what gets attention first. Your email-manager skill triages your inbox — it separates messages that need a real reply from noise you can ignore.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

hubspot.title: HubSpot
hubspot.content: A CRM and marketing platform used by sales, marketing, and customer success teams. Common target for AI automations — students connect it to draft outreach, enrich contacts, or sync data with other tools.

trigger.title: Trigger
trigger.content: The event that kicks off an automation, like 'new email received' or 'row added to a sheet.' Every Zapier or n8n workflow starts with a trigger and then runs the actions that follow.

voice-guide.title: Voice Guide
voice-guide.content: A file that captures how you write — your tone, vocabulary, sentence structure, and preferences. Share it with Claude so it writes in your style instead of generic AI voice.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: 48% of UK consumers, and 42% across EMEA, say they'd think less of a brand whose advertising ran next to poor-quality, spam-like AI-generated content, per DoubleVerify's 2026 Global Insights report on media quality. This system runs before a draft goes anywhere near a reader. It scores the draft against your brand [voice guide](#tooltip-voice-guide) and flags the specific lines that read generic, off-tone, or unsupported.

"AI slop" is now its own named risk category, one that ad-quality vendors and industry groups benchmark directly instead of leaving it to a copywriter's complaint. A rubric a person can run quickly catches what a style guide nobody rereads never does. The check quotes the exact phrase and the rule it breaks, so whoever approves the draft can fix it before a reader flags it for them.
Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) before publish, a saved [AI skill](#tooltip-skill) your team reuses, or a gate wired into your publishing tool.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming where your voice guide lives, what counts as a hard violation versus a softer drift, and who sees the results before something goes out.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that scores any piece of copy against our brand voice guide before it ships. Ask me questions, one at a time, about where our voice guide lives, what the most common ways our copy drifts off-voice actually are, what should automatically fail the check versus just get flagged, and who needs to see the results before something goes out. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to name the difference between a hard violation and a soft drift before you've built anything, so the check doesn't flag everything or nothing.

items: Where your brand voice guide lives, and whether it's current enough to check against.
What counts as a hard violation, banned words or off-brand claims, versus a softer stylistic drift worth flagging but not blocking.
Whether this runs as a manual paste-and-check step or a gate wired into your publishing tool.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather what it calls for: the brand voice guide file, a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) to your publishing or scheduling tool (Buffer, WordPress, [HubSpot](#tooltip-hubspot)) if you want the check wired in as a gate, and your review channel ([Slack](#tooltip-slack)). The paste-in version needs nothing beyond the guide and the draft.
**Create.** Build your system and test it on a real draft, with the guide attached. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document gives a version for your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Score this draft against our brand voice guide and flag specific problems.

Context: Here is our brand voice guide: [paste or link the guide]. Here is the draft to check: [paste it].

Rules:
- Quote the exact phrase you're flagging, don't just describe the problem generally.
- Distinguish between a hard violation (banned words, off-brand claims) and a softer stylistic drift.
- Do not rewrite the draft yourself, this is a check, not an edit.
- Output format: a pass/needs-revision verdict, then a list of flagged lines with the exact quote, the rule it breaks, and a one-line reason.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: requiring the exact quoted phrase for every flag keeps the check specific enough to act on instead of a vague sense that something's off.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Exact quotes, hard violations kept separate from soft drift, no rewrite attempted?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly which flag missed and fold the correction into the rules.

items: Add a severity score so reviewers [triage](#tooltip-triage) fast.
Track which rules [trigger](#tooltip-trigger) most often and use that to sharpen the guide itself.
Extend the same rubric to outbound emails and ad copy alongside long-form content.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) instead of a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each brand voice check, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, draft checked, flags raised, flags overridden, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make it visible after a few weeks whether the check is catching real problems or just adding noise.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a couple weeks straight, package the prompt and rules into a skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill writes it for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. Vague rules like "sound more human" produce vague flags nobody can act on, so keep every rule specific enough to quote an exact violation.
